intro.title: 1. Introduction to Pluto
intro.html:
Introduction

Pluto is not just a drone, it is a development tool. It enables the user to develop numerous projects across different areas. With the Pluto Platform, you can create and innovate to bring your ideas into reality.

From simply glowing LEDs, to understanding complicated scientific concepts, to developing fun games - everything is possible with the Pluto Platform. The sensor data and the remote control data are all accessible with this platform, making it one of a kind.

With the platform being open source, tinkering is made a lot easier with the API based coding in C++. And if you have never coded in your life, we have something for you as well - Pluto Blocks.

Pluto Blocks is an easy drag and drop block programming application which does not require any prior knowledge of programming languages. It provides a comprehensible platform to tinker with Pluto 1.2 and Pluto X nano drones. With PlutoBlocks, we aim to motivate the users to begin their journey into the universe of drones. Some of the key features of Pluto Blocks are:

  • Easy drag and drop blocks
  • Real time C++ code in separate tab helps in learning the programming language
  • No separate software required to build and flash the code
  • Wireless flashing makes everything much easier and faster
  • User friendly UI makes it exciting for users of all ages

platform.title: 3. Platform Overview
platform.html:
The Pluto platform consists of three essential components: Hardware, Software, and Design. All three are crucial for smooth, safe flying, and each can be customized for your own projects—making Pluto a flexible tool for learning, building, and innovating.

Component Role
Hardware All of the electronics and mechanical parts needed to make and control the drone
Software All flight logic, communication, and APIs for programming
Design The frame/structure, customizable for new ideas or extra components

primus.title: 3.1 Primus – Hardware (X2 / V5)
primus.html:
All Pluto drones use the Primus flight controller as the core hardware. Pluto X has Primus X2 v1 and Pluto 1.2 has Primus V4. Both are capable, modern "brains" for your drone.

magis.title: 3.2 Magis – The Software
magis.html:
Hardware is just the start Magis (the software) is what brings Pluto to life.
Most users never need to program Pluto for basic flight: the preloaded Magis firmware already delivers stable, reliable control.

If you want to understand how Magis keeps flights stable, break it down by logical blocks. Knowing what each block does makes experimenting easier.

Pluto runs the MagisV2-API-Library firmware, with different blocks for data, estimation, control, and hardware interfaces.

Core Flight Control Blocks

These blocks are responsible for essential flying functions:

  1. FC-Data: Reads and processes the drone's sensor data.
    Sensors: Accelerometer (X, Y, Z, Net_Acc), Gyroscope (X, Y, Z), Magnetometer (X, Y, Z), Barometer (Pressure, Temp).
    Filters: Cleans raw data (e.g., Complementary Filter).
    Estimate: Calculates actual state (angles, rates, position, velocity).
  2. FC-Config: Holds important settings (loop frequency, PID gains).
  3. FC-Control: Main flight logic, mode switching, and taking user commands (ARM/DISARM, status, remote/app conversion, flight modes, HeadFree heading, etc).
  4. Motors: Converts control signals to motor output. (Standard: M5–M8; Bi-directional: M1–M2 with special setup)

Supporting & Peripheral Blocks

  1. BMS: Battery health, current/voltage, mAh tracking.
  2. Peripherals & Serial: GPIO, ADC, PWM ports & protocols (I2C, SPI, UART).
  3. Add-Ons: Expansion hardware (OLED, distance sensors, etc).
  4. Debugging: Print and graph APIs for real-time monitoring.

Tip: Focus on one logical block at a time when learning or tinkering it’s easier and more fun!

p0.title: Project 0
p0.html:
Challenge

Build a project to turn the Red LED ON.

Solution

Running the project:

⇀ Build and flash the project (Refer Building and Flashing section for steps)

⇀ Connect the Pluto Controller App with the drone and turn the Developer Mode ON to execute the project

⇀ The Red LED will turn ON

⇀ The LED will turn OFF when the Developer Mode will be turned OFF

REMEMBER:

⇀ All the projects have to be built and flashed in the same manner

⇀ The projects will run in the Developer Mode only

After understanding Project 0, let us try more block programming with the help of the next projects. We recommend you to first try building the projects on your own by reading the challenge and later refer to the solution to review your project.

Challenge:

Solution:

p2.title: Project 2
p2.html:
Challenge

Build a program such that if the Pitch input from the Pluto Controller App (RC Pitch) is greater than 1500, the Red LED should turn ON. If the value is less than 1500, the Red LED should turn OFF.

Solution

Pro Tip:

You do not need to fly or arm the drone to execute this project. This project works even when the drone is on the ground. Try moving the Pitch slider in the Pluto Controller App and observe the Red LED.

p3.title: Project 3
p3.html:
Challenge

Build a program such that if the Pitch input from the Pluto Controller App (RC Pitch) is greater than 1500, the Red LED should turn ON. If the value is less than 1500, the Green LED should turn ON.

Solution

Pro Tip:

Remember to turn the first LED OFF before turning the other LED ON. If an LED is not turned OFF, it will remain ON along with the second LED. Try testing this behavior to understand LED state control better.

p4.title: Project 4
p4.html:
Challenge

Build a program such that the Blue LED will TOGGLE after every 2 seconds.

Solution

Pro Tip

Toggle means changing the current state.

If the LED is ON, it turns OFF. If it is OFF, it turns ON.

The LED will switch its state every 2 seconds.

Try changing the timer duration and observe how the behavior changes to better understand how the timer block works.

p5.title: Project 5
p5.html:
Challenge

Build a program to blink an LED after every 2 seconds.

Solution

Pro Tip

If the LED is not switched OFF, it will remain ON continuously and will not blink.

This program turns the LED ON every 2 seconds and then switches it OFF to create a blinking effect.

Try changing the time to a very small value and observe how fast the LED blinks.

p6.title: Project 6
p6.html:
Challenge

Build a program such that all motors receive 1200 PWM when Developer Mode is ON, and all motors receive 1000 PWM when Developer Mode is OFF.

Solution

Pro Tip

Whenever you control motors using PWM, always shut them OFF by setting 1000 PWM inside On Stop.

This ensures motors do not keep running when Developer Mode is turned OFF or when the app gets disconnected.

p7.title: Project 7
p7.html:
Challenge

Build a program such that the Green LED and Blue LED turn ON and the drone yaws to 150 degrees.
Hint: Use the Desired Yaw block.

Solution

Pro Tip

The execution of Desired State blocks (like Desired Yaw) can be tested only while flying the drone.

Make sure the drone is armed and airborne before checking the yaw behavior.

p8.title: Project 8
p8.html:

Build a program such that if the current Roll angle is between -180° and 0°, the Red LED turns ON, and if the Roll angle is between 0° and 180°, the Green LED turns ON.

p9.title: Project 1: Color Wheel
p9.html:
Challenge

As the drone yaws through 360°, it should generate different primary and secondary colors using the onboard LEDs.

The Idea

A color wheel shows how primary colors combine to form secondary colors. In this project, you will turn your Pluto into a live color wheel and visually observe how LED colors blend as the yaw angle changes.

Approach

The Primus V4 / Primus X flight controller has Red, Green, and Blue LEDs. By turning ON different combinations of these LEDs at specific yaw angle ranges, you can generate secondary colors.

If the LEDs are conditioned based on the current yaw angle of the drone, Pluto behaves like a rotating color wheel.

Code

Insights

⇀ Magnetometer is the most important sensor for measuring the Yaw angle.

⇀ If yaw values are unstable, perform Magnetometer Calibration from the Pluto Controller App.

⇀ This project does not require flying or arming the drone.

p10.title: Project 2: Compass Drone
p10.html:
Challenge

Use your Pluto drone as a compass to point towards the North, East, South, and West directions.

The Idea

Compasses have been used since ancient times to determine direction. A standard compass points towards North. With this project, you will convert your Pluto into a digital compass that can point to North, East, South, West—or any direction you choose.

Approach

When the drone is properly Magnetometer calibrated, a yaw angle of 0° corresponds to the North direction.

  • 0° → North
  • 90° → East
  • 180° → South
  • 270° → West

By setting the desired yaw angle of the drone to these values, Pluto can be made to point in specific directions. As a visual indicator, you can use different LEDs for different directions.

Code

Activity

⇀ Along with a few friends, try guessing directions inside a room with no sunlight.

⇀ Use this project to verify the actual directions.

⇀ The person with the closest guess wins!

p11.title: Project 3: Spirit Level
p11.html:
Challenge

Build a program to use Pluto as a digital spirit level and detect whether a surface is perfectly horizontal.

The Idea

Traditional spirit levels are used to check if a surface is horizontal or vertical. With Pluto, you can upgrade this age-old tool by using the drone’s sensors and LEDs to make a smart, customizable spirit level.

Approach

Pluto’s sensors provide real-time values of Roll, Pitch, and Yaw angles. By using the current Roll angle and controlling the onboard LEDs, you can indicate whether a surface is level.

  • If the Roll angle is outside a defined range, LEDs should blink
  • If the surface is perfectly horizontal, a steady LED should indicate balance
  • Adjust the loop time to control LED toggle frequency

Solution

Insights

⇀ Changing the loop time affects how fast the LED blinks

⇀ Accuracy can be customized by modifying the acceptable angle

p12.title: Project 4: Truth or Dare
p12.html:
Challenge

Build a fun game where a spinning drone replaces the traditional spinning bottle to play Truth or Dare.

The Idea

In the classic Truth or Dare game, a bottle is spun to randomly select a participant. In this upgraded version, the Pluto drone itself spins and points toward a participant when it stops. The selected person must then choose between Truth or Dare.

Approach

Pluto Blocks allows you to set the desired yaw angle of the drone. The drone will rotate to whichever yaw angle you command.

  • Use a random yaw angle to create surprise
  • Use a timer block so the drone gets enough time to reach an angle before receiving the next command
  • Fly the drone in Headfree mode for easier control

Solution

Game Rules

⇀ Play with 4 participants

⇀ Each participant stands at 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270° relative to the drone

⇀ When the drone stops spinning, the person it points to must choose Truth or Dare

Activity

Modify the code so the game can be played by 6 participants instead of 4. Think about how yaw angles should be divided equally!

p13.title: Project 5: Chuck to Arm
p13.html:
Challenge

Build a program to arm the drone automatically when it is tossed in the air.

The Idea

Normally, a drone is armed while resting on the ground. In this project, you will arm Pluto by simply throwing it into the air, making the arming process more intuitive and fun.

Approach

When the drone is tossed upward, it enters a brief free-fall condition. During this moment, the accelerometer’s Net Acceleration value drops close to zero.

  • Detect when Net Acceleration ≈ 0
  • Ensure the condition is not caused by a crash
  • Arm the drone instantly at that moment

Important: The drone must be armed from the app before executing this project.

Solution

Pro Tip

⇀ Toss the drone gently—do not throw it aggressively

⇀ Always perform this project in an open, safe area

⇀ Understanding free-fall detection is useful for advanced flight logic

p14.title: Project 6: Open Sesame
p14.html:
Challenge

Build a program such that the drone takes off when air is blown on it, using the onboard Barometer sensor.

The Idea

Instead of using the Take Off button in the Pluto Controller App, you will use the Barometer sensor present on the Primus V4 / Primus X board. Blowing air on the drone causes a sudden change in air pressure, which can be used as a trigger to take off.

Approach

The Barometer continuously measures air pressure. When air is blown over the sensor, a temporary pressure spike or dip is detected.

  • Monitor the current pressure value
  • Detect a sudden change compared to the initial pressure
  • Trigger takeoff when the threshold is crossed

Important: Always arm the drone from the app before running this project.

Solution

Activity

⇀ Place the drone near a door

⇀ Open or close the door quickly to generate airflow

⇀ Observe the drone take off due to the pressure change

p15.title: Project 7: Gyroscopic Drone
p15.html:
Challenge

Experience the effect of the Gyroscope sensor by powering the motors using only gyroscope data while holding Pluto in your hand.

The Idea

The Gyroscope is one of the most important sensors used in devices ranging from smartphones to submarines and even space telescopes. In this project, you will understand how the gyroscope works by directly experiencing its effect through motor response.

Approach

Instead of using multiple sensors, this project relies only on gyroscope data to control the motors.

  • Read gyroscope values in real time
  • Positive gyro values power one set of motors
  • Negative gyro values power the opposite set of motors

This makes the motors respond instantly to rotational motion of the drone.

Experiment

Solution

Activity

⇀ Try changing the inclination of Pluto about the roll axis without making the motors rotate

⇀ This must be done very slowly, demonstrating how gyroscopes measure rate of rotation

p16.title: Project 8: Logic Drone
p16.html:
Challenge

Understand the working of basic Logic Gates (AND / OR) by using Pluto as a physical logic demonstration system.

The Idea

Logic Gates form the foundation of all digital electronics. Pluto Blocks provides logical operators such as AND and OR, allowing you to visualize how logic works using real inputs and outputs.

Approach

The Pluto Controller App itself is used to provide inputs:

  • Throttle stick and Pitch stick act as logic inputs
  • AND logic: Throttle UP AND Pitch UP
  • OR logic: Throttle DOWN OR Pitch DOWN

Based on the logic result, all four motors are powered and different LED combinations are activated.

Inputs

Solution

Insight: This project shows how abstract logic operations directly control physical systems like motors and LEDs.

p17.title: Project 9: One Key Return
p17.html:
Challenge

Build a program to call the drone back to the pilot using Developer Mode, without using GPS.

The Idea

This project demonstrates how a drone can return to its owner by tracking the phone's heading instead of relying on GPS technology. When the drone flies far away, Developer Mode can be used as a single command to bring it back.

Approach

The Pluto Controller App continuously sends the phone’s heading (Yaw). By comparing the drone’s heading with the phone’s heading, the drone can rotate and move toward the pilot.

  • Use phone heading data sent from the app
  • Calculate the difference between drone heading and phone heading
  • Adjust yaw to face the pilot
  • Move forward to return

Solution

Important Notes

  • Connect the drone using PlutoBlocks
  • Turn ON Send Heading in Developer Settings
  • Create Integers: DroneHead, phoneYaw, Read
  • Create Boolean: Flag

p18.title: Project 1: Hooter Module
p18.html:
Introduction

Pluto X supports many add-ons. One useful add-on is the Hooter Module (buzzer). In this project, you will connect a buzzer to your Pluto drone to make it beep.

Challenge

Create a program that lets your Pluto drone make a beeping sound using the buzzer module.

Add-On Used

The buzzer module makes sound when it gets power. It is used for alerts or beeps.

Connection

Connect the buzzer module to the RC port on the Primus V5 / X2 board as shown:

  • GND → GND
  • Signal → VCC

Solution

How it works:
- When the program starts, set the GPIO_1 (Pin 1) LOW and start a timer for 1 second.
- In the main loop, when the timer is true, GPIO_1 is set HIGH to turn ON the buzzer, then LOW to turn it OFF. This makes the buzzer beep repeatedly.
- When stopping, reset the timer.

What it Looks Like

Try This!

⇀ Use a sensor to change beep timing

⇀ Make it beep Morse code for a word!
